Single or Multiple Policies for Phase-Structured Reinforcement Learning?

Guilhem Loussouarn    Nancy Nayak    Kin K. Leung Affiliation: Department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering Affiliation: Imperial College London, UK
Abstract

Many reinforcement-learning (RL) problems are non-stationary yet structured and can be decomposed into phases, each with its own transition probabilities and reward functions. When the phase sequence is known, the common solution augments the state with information to satisfy the Markovian property and applies standard RL techniques. However, prior work finds that the multi-policy approach for different phases can outperform a single state-augmented policy shared among the phases, for reasons that remain unclear. In this work, we first show that the shared policy can theoretically achieve performance of any multi-policy solution. However, whether a multi-policy solution can perform better than the corresponding single shared policy in practice depends on function approximation, learning and optimization processes, as well as, for multi-policy solutions, the sample efficiency and loss of continuity from one policy to another. We propose a regime-based phase decomposition method to identify which policy can provide better performance. The method is based on consideration of the duration of transient system dynamics relative to the duration of the quasi-stationary period. Numerical experiments are conducted with different non-stationary RL problems to validate our four major hypotheses: (a) longer phase durations favor multi-policies, (b) the heterogeneity between phases increases the burden on single policy, (c) multi-policies need sufficient data for each phase, and (d) environment-specific transition dynamics between phases can affect which policy is preferable.

1 Introduction

Many sequential decision-making problems are non-stationary but exhibit recurring structure. Their transition dynamics or rewards may change between a finite set of phases. Within a phase, the interactions are described by a stationary Markov decision process (MDP) with phase-specific transitions and rewards; across phases, these MDPs are coupled, since the actions taken in one phase determine the state from which the next begins. We call the resulting sequence of coupled MDPs a phase-structured MDP. Examples include daily traffic and demand cycles (Mucelli Rezende Oliveira et al., 2017; Shi and Li, 2018; Haffey et al., 2018; Dán and Carlsson, 2014), robotic contact modes (Kroemer et al., 2021), and changing computational workloads (Amvrosiadis et al., 2018). We focus on deterministic scheduled phases, allowing both periodic and arbitrary fixed non-periodic structures, in which the active phase is observed. A latent or history-dependent phase process must instead be inferred from interaction, making the problem partially observable, and we leave that case to future work.

State augmentation restores a time-homogeneous MDP only when the appended statistic is sufficient for both the physical dynamics and the evolution of the schedule (Puterman, 1994). For a periodic schedule, the phase index and local clock are sufficient. More general schedules may require additional scheduler information, such as global time or the position within a known sequence. This resolves how the process is represented, but not how policy parameters should be shared across phases. We distinguish three primary architectures along a parameter-sharing spectrum (Figure 1c): a shared policy uses one phase-conditioned network for all phases; a multi-policy architecture uses an independent specialist for each phase; and a multi-head policy shares a representation but uses phase-specific output heads.

Recent work on periodic network resource allocation found that multipolicy PPO can outperform a shared state-augmented policy (Chen et al., 2025). If the active phase is already observed by the shared policy, why should separate policies help? At the level of unrestricted policy classes, they should not: a shared phase-conditioned policy can reproduce any collection of phase-specific policies, so the advantage of specialization cannot follow from expressivity alone, nor does it imply that specialization is always preferable. How much information and how many parameters are shared nonetheless affects learning performance, sample efficiency, and computational cost. We therefore ask: when should a policy share parameters across phases, and when should it specialize?

Central claim. Under finite learning resources, specialization is favoured when its phase-local learning benefit exceeds the costs of sample fragmentation and boundary handoff. Sharing is favoured when transfer, data pooling, and cross-phase coordination dominate.

We relate this trade-off to three properties of a phase-structured MDP. First, phase heterogeneity determines how different the behaviours required in each phase are. Second, the training budget determines whether every specialist receives enough data to learn its phase. Third, the within-phase regime structure determines the importance of coordination. Immediately after a phase change, performance may depend strongly on the state inherited from the previous phase. We call this the transient regime. Once this dependence has weakened, the phase enters a quasi-stationary regime in which phase-local specialization may be more beneficial. The duration of the transient and its sensitivity to the inherited state determine the handoff cost of independent policies.

We study these mechanisms under observable phase structure, leaving latent phase inference outside our scope. Across our three environments, changing the phase count, duration, heterogeneity, budget, or boundary dependence can reverse the ranking of shared and specialized architectures. Our contributions are fivefold. First, we formalize phase-structured MDPs and identify the scheduler state that restores a time-homogeneous MDP. Second, we show that the shared phase-conditioned policy class is equivalent to the multipolicy class, so any performance difference between them is a learning effect rather than a representational one. Third, we split each phase occurrence into transient and quasi-stationary regimes and decompose the learned return gap into a settled specialization gain and a transient handoff cost, yielding a phase-wise rule for when specialization pays and tying the gain to phase heterogeneity and the per-phase sample budget. Fourth, we derive diagnostics linking architecture choice to phase heterogeneity, phase-local sample budgets, transient duration, and handoff sensitivity. Finally, we test these predictions with single shared, multihead, and multipolicy PPO on HAPS coverage control, PhasePendulum, and PhaseGridWorld, and probe the proposed mechanisms through capacity controls, gradient measurements, warm starts, distillation, and controlled handoff interventions.

Paper roadmap. The remainder of this paper follows the conceptual flow outlined in Figure 1. Section 2 situates our approach within the broader literature on non-stationary RL, multi-task learning, and capacity. Section 3 formalizes phase-structured MDPs and the policy class equivalence. Section 4 proposes the regime decomposition into transient and quasi-stationary phases (Figure 1a) and derives the diagnostic metrics quantifying handoff costs, settled gains, and sample budgets (Figure 1b). Finally, Section 5 validates these predictions experimentally across three environments, demonstrating how competing mechanisms propose an appropriate level of sharing of architectural components across different architectures(Figure 1c).

2 Related Work

Structured time-varying MDPs. Prior work studies MDPs whose transition and reward functions change according to an underlying structure. Periodic MDPs assume that these changes repeat on a fixed cycle and commonly include the period index in the state to use state-augmented policies (Riis, 1965; Veugen et al., 1983; Podtsykin, 1991; Osogami and Raymond, 2014; Hu and Defourny, 2014; Aniket and Chattopadhyay, 2023). Other models consider stochastic or hidden changes, such as switching non-stationary MDPs governed by a latent Markov chain (Amiri and Magnússon, 2026). We use phase-structured MDP to refer broadly to the cases when the change structure is deterministic and observed. Sec. 3 provides the formal definition. As for phase-structured RL, it represents the full range of RL methods applied to phase-structured MDPs.

Periodic multi-policy reinforcement learning. (Chen et al., 2025) propose multi-policy RL for periodic network resource allocation and report gains over single-policy baselines. A related multi-policy architecture has been applied to high-altitude platform system (HAPS) control in a phase-structured telecommunications environment (Loussouarn et al., 2026) with similar improvements. In both cases, no explanations on the gap between state-augmented policy and multi-policy performances are given. We take these empirical observations as motivation and study the architectural choice between parameter sharing and phase specialization across controlled domains. Our HAPS benchmark retains the coverage-control component of the latter environment, enabling systematic ablations of the factors governing this choice.

Multi-task learning, modularity, and transfer. Multi-task learning aims to solve related tasks jointly by sharing parameters or representations (Caruana, 1997). Phase-structured RL admits a similar interpretation: the phase acts as a task descriptor, a state-augmented policy shares all parameters across phases, and a multipolicy uses independent phase specialists. Sharing can improve data efficiency through transfer, but it can also cause negative transfer when tasks require incompatible updates. PCGrad and CAGrad modify task gradients to reduce such conflicts (Yu et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2021); we evaluate them as baselines and use phase-specific gradient geometry as a local diagnostic.

Modular and transfer methods address limitations of complete sharing or separation. Mixture-of-experts models divide complex mappings among specialized modules (Jacobs et al., 1991; Jordan and Jacobs, 1994). Divide-and-conquer RL uses local policies to simplify difficult optimization, while distillation, Distral, progressive networks, and generalist–specialist learning transfer or preserve knowledge across policies and tasks (Ghosh et al., 2018; Rusu et al., 2015; Teh et al., 2017; Rusu et al., 2016; Jia et al., 2022). These ideas motivate our multihead and warm-start baselines, which we define in Sec. 5.

The analogy remains incomplete because standard multi-task formulations generally sample tasks separately (Zeng et al., 2021). Phases are instead consecutive parts of one trajectory: the policy used in one phase determines the state passed to the next. Existing multi-task methods therefore address sharing and transfer, but not necessarily cross-phase coordination.

Capacity and irrelevant features. Network size and training compute can affect deep-RL performance, although their benefits depend on the algorithm, environment, and data regime (Hilton et al., 2023; Schwarzer et al., 2023; Rybkin et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2025). Moreover, observations that are irrelevant to the optimal decision can still increase the difficulty of finite-sample learning with function approximation (Jong and Stone, 2004). These observations motivate our capacity and distractor controls, which test whether multi-policy gains can be explained by parameter count or by the difficulty of extracting phase information.

3 Phase-Structured MDPs

We begin by recalling the standard MDP formulation. An MDP is a tuple 𝒫=(𝒮,𝒜,p,r,μ0,γ)\mathcal{P}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},p,r,\mu_{0},\gamma), where 𝒮\mathcal{S} and 𝒜\mathcal{A} are the state and action spaces, p(⋅∣s,a)p(\cdot\mid s,a) is the state-transition probability distribution (or transition kernel), r⁡(s,a)r(s,a) is the expected one-step reward, μ0\mu_{0} is the initial-state distribution, and γ∈(0,1]\gamma\in(0,1] is the discount factor.

Phases and schedules. Let ℳ={0,…,M−1}\mathcal{M}=\{0,\ldots,M-1\} be a finite set of phases. Each phase m∈ℳm\in\mathcal{M} identifies a stationary mode of the environment, described by a transition probability distribution pmp_{m} and reward function rmr_{m}. A phase is therefore a model of the local dynamics and objective. A deterministic phase schedule is a map σ:ℕ→ℳ,\sigma:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow\mathcal{M}, and σ⁡(t)\sigma(t) denotes the phase active at time tt. For example, consider the sequence of phases mm in Table 1 consisting of four phases m∈ℳ={0,1,2,3}m\in\mathcal{M}=\{0,1,2,3\} that may occur multiple times in an episode. The total duration of the occurrence of each phase is arbitrary, i.e., the duration of the first occurrence (j=0)(j=0) of phase m=0m=0 is two time steps, i.e. Tm,j|m=0,j=0=2T_{m,j}|_{m=0,j=0}=2, whereas the second occurrence (j=1)(j=1) of phase m=0m=0 is only one time step, i.e., Tm,j|m=0,j=1=1T_{m,j}|_{m=0,j=1}=1. τ⁡(t)\tau(t) denotes the local time step within a phase.

Definition 1 (Phase-structured MDP).

A deterministic phase-structured MDP is a tuple
𝒫σ=(𝒮,𝒜,{pm}m∈ℳ,{rm}m∈ℳ,μ0,γ,σ).\mathcal{P}_{\sigma}=\left(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\{p_{m}\}_{m\in\mathcal{M}},\{r_{m}\}_{m\in\mathcal{M}},\mu_{0},\gamma,\sigma\right). At time tt, the active phase is σ⁡(t)\sigma(t) and starting from an initial state s0∼μ0s_{0}\sim\mu_{0}, the process evolves at time tt according to

st+1∼pσ⁡(t)(⋅∣st,at),rt=rσ⁡(t)(st,at).s_{t+1}\sim p_{\sigma(t)}(\cdot\mid s_{t},a_{t}),\qquad r_{t}=r_{\sigma(t)}(s_{t},a_{t}).

For a finite horizon NN, the objective is to find an optimal policy π∗\pi^{*} such that:

π⋆∈arg⁡maxπ​JN​(π), where ​JN​(π)=𝔼μ0,π,σ​[∑t=0N−1γt​rσ⁡(t)​(st,at)].\pi^{\star}\in\arg\max_{\pi}J_{N}(\pi),\quad\text{ where }J_{N}(\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{0},\pi,\sigma}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{N-1}\gamma^{t}r_{\sigma(t)}(s_{t},a_{t})\right].

The expectation is taken over the initial state, policy actions, and state transitions under the fixed schedule σ\sigma. For an infinite horizon, we take N=∞N=\infty and assume γ<1\gamma<1 and bounded rewards.

Scheduler state and Markovianity. The state sts_{t} alone may not be Markov. For the same state, the transition or reward can differ depending on the active phase σ⁡(t)\sigma(t). Let zt=(σ⁡(t),it)z_{t}=(\sigma(t),i_{t}) denote the scheduler state, where σ⁡(t)\sigma(t) is the phase index and iti_{t} is auxiliary schedule context. We call ztz_{t} sufficient if transition dynamics depend on history solely through (st,at,zt)(s_{t},a_{t},z_{t}). In practice, observing only σ⁡(t)\sigma(t) is insufficient because phase dynamics vary internally over time. While appending global time (it=ti_{t}=t) technically restores Markovianity, it transforms the state space into an acyclic directed graph that prevents data re-use across cycles. To preserve both Markovian sufficiency and sample efficiency, iti_{t} must be mapped to a compact quotient space; for periodic phases of length TmT_{m}, the within-phase clock τ⁡(t)=tmodTm\tau(t)=t\bmod T_{m} suffices (zt=(σ⁡(t),τ⁡(t))z_{t}=(\sigma(t),\tau(t)); see App. A.1.1).

Proposition 1 (Scheduler-state augmentation).

If ztz_{t} is sufficient, then the augmented state s~t=(st,zt)\widetilde{s}_{t}=(s_{t},z_{t}) defines a time-homogeneous MDP and recovers Markovianity.

The formal Markovian sufficiency conditions and a periodic phase schedule (Corr. 1) are detailed in App. A.1.1. The proofs of Cor. 1 and Prop. 1 are detailed in App. A.2).

Phase-local models and handoffs. For a phase mm and an entry-state distribution μ\mu, define the stationary phase-local model

𝒫m​(μ)=(𝒮,𝒜,pmπ,rm,μ,γ),\mathcal{P}_{m}(\mu)=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},p_{m}^{\pi},r_{m},\mu,\gamma), (1)

which describes the local dynamics and rewards. In a phase-structured MDP, however, μ\mu is not fixed, i.e., the distribution μm,jπ\mu_{m,j}^{\pi} of the state at the start of the jt​hj^{th} occurrence of phase mm is induced by the actions π\pi in the preceding phases. The state transition probabilities pmπp_{m}^{\pi} therefore are also dependent on previous policies π\pi such that pmπ=∑a∈𝒜pm​(st+1|at,st)​π​(at|st)p_{m}^{\pi}=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}p_{m}(s_{t+1}|a_{t},s_{t})\pi(a_{t}|s_{t}). The phases therefore cannot in general be treated as independent. This cross-phase dependence is the handoff effect studied in Sec. 4.

Shared policy and specialized policies. Since the augmented state s~t\tilde{s}_{t} yields a time-homogeneous MDP, standard RL methods can learn a single policy π\pi across all phases. We call any such policy a shared policy. Instead, (Chen et al., 2025) train a separate specialized policy for each phase, an architecture shown to outperform shared policies in phase-structured problems. Yet, specialized policies hold no representational advantage, since any set of them can be expressed by a single shared policy.

Proposition 2 (Shared–multipolicy equivalence).

There is a bijection between shared policies πsh(⋅∣s,i,m)\pi^{\text{sh}}(\cdot\mid s,i,m) and an ensemble of specialized policies 𝛑sp=(π0(⋅∣s,i),…,πM−1(⋅∣s,i))\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\textbf{sp}}=(\pi_{0}(\cdot\mid s,i),\ldots,\pi_{M-1}(\cdot\mid s,i)) expressed through the gated map Γ\Gamma such that

πsp​(a∣s,i,m)=Γ⁡(𝝅sp)​(a∣s,i,m)=πm​(a∣s,i),\displaystyle\pi^{\rm sp}(a\mid s,i,m)=\Gamma(\boldsymbol{\pi}^{\textbf{sp}})(a\mid s,i,m)=\pi_{m}(a\mid s,i), (2)
πsh​(a∣s,i,m)=πm​(a∣s,i)=πsp​(a∣s,i,m).\displaystyle\pi^{\text{sh}}(a\mid s,i,m)=\pi_{m}(a\mid s,i)=\pi^{\text{sp}}(a\mid s,i,m).

It is always possible to represent a shared policy with an ensemble of specialized policies and vice versa.

This is a policy-class equivalence: with unrestricted function classes, shared and specialized policies attain the same optimal return. However, it says nothing about where each architecture reaches when trained. With finite networks, finite data, and gradient-based optimization, the two can converge to different solutions, which is why either may outperform the other in practice. The next section characterizes when specialization is preferable to sharing, and when the reverse holds. Illustrations and proof of Prop. 2 can be found inside App. A.2

4 When to Share and When to Specialize

Each phase-local model 𝒫m​(μ)\mathcal{P}_{m}(\mu) introduced in (1) is stationary within its phase horizon but inherits its initial entry distribution μ\mu from the preceding phases. We now ask how long that inheritance matters within a phase, and how the answer, together with the heterogeneity of consecutive phases, determines whether a shared or a specialized policy is better suited.

4.1 Transient and Quasi-Stationary Regimes

At a phase boundary, an inherited condition such as position, velocity, network load, or other initial-state condition can strongly affect subsequent performance. We call the period during which performance remains sensitive to this inherited state the transient regime, and the remaining steps, once the sensitivity has become small, the quasi-stationary regime, in which behaviour is governed mainly by the current phase’s dynamics and objective. Quasi-stationarity does not require convergence to an invariant state distribution. It requires only that the effect of the entry state on the return quantities under study has become small.

Let Lm,j≤Tm,jL_{m,j}\leq T_{m,j} denote the duration of the transient regime of the jt​hj^{th} occurrence of phase mm, leaving a quasi-stationary regime of duration Tm,j−Lm,jT_{m,j}-L_{m,j} time steps. Occurrences of the same phase may differ in Lm,jL_{m,j} because they inherit different entry distributions, and in slowly mixing or disconnected systems the transient may span the whole phase (Lm,j=Tm,jL_{m,j}=T_{m,j}), so periodicity alone does not guarantee recovery before the next boundary. We estimate Lm,jL_{m,j} from phase-age behaviour and properties of the environment. App. A.1.2 gives the formal recovery definition and the occurrence-level aggregation.

The two regimes expose different architectural trade-offs. In the quasi-stationary regime, independent training may make a phase-local mapping easier to approximate and optimize than a joint mapping across all phases. In the transient regime, policies remain coupled through the state passed across the boundary. A shared policy trained on complete trajectories can account for this continuation value, whereas independently trained phase-local specialized policies may not. Sharing also pools data and reuses representations, whereas a balanced specialized policy receives only about B/MB/M of a total budget BB. We now quantify these effects.

4.2 Settled Gains and Transient Handoff Costs

The regime decomposition explains why the preferred architecture may vary across phase-structured problems; we now make that comparison quantitative. We measure the gain phase-specific learning obtains in the quasi-stationary regime against the cost specialization incurs in the transient regime, which together form the architecture diagnostic developed in the next subsection.

A comparison between learned shared and learned specialized policies. Let the learned shared and the learned specialized policies are denoted by π^sh\widehat{\pi}^{\rm sh} and π^sp\widehat{\pi}^{\rm sp}, respectively. For occurrence jj of phase mm, with a transient regime duration of Lm,j≤Tm,jL_{m,j}\leq T_{m,j}, define λm,j=∑t=0Lm,j−1γt/∑t=0Tm,j−1γt\lambda_{m,j}=\sum_{t=0}^{L_{m,j}-1}\gamma^{t}/\sum_{t=0}^{T_{m,j}-1}\gamma^{t}. Thus λm,j\lambda_{m,j} is the fraction of the occurrence’s discounted mass assigned to the transient regime. Let J¯m,j,Atr\bar{J}_{m,j,A}^{\rm tr} and J¯m,j,Aqs\bar{J}_{m,j,A}^{\rm qs} denote the discounted average rewards of architecture A∈{sh,sp}A\in\{\mathrm{sh},\mathrm{sp}\} for single shared and specialized policies, in the transient and quasi-stationary windows. where ωm\omega_{m} is the fraction of discounted evaluation mass belonging to phase mm. The derivation of the above formulation is given in detail in App. A.1.2. (1−λm)​Gm>λm​Km.(1-\lambda_{m})G_{m}>\lambda_{m}K_{m}. (5)

Transient hand off cost KmK_{m}. The entry law μm,A\mu_{m,A} is produced by the policy acting in the phase before mm, and no architecture removes this coupling. Standard multi-policy training optimizes each specialized policy on phase-local experience, so a specialist may miss how its late actions shift the entry state of the next phase, whereas a shared policy trained on complete trajectories receives that cross-phase credit. Accordingly, KmK_{m} is large when achievable return is sensitive to the entry state and recovery is slow; and small when entry distributions match, dynamics contract quickly, or phases reset independently.

Quasi-stationary gain GmG_{m}. In the quasi-stationary regime, phase mm resembles its phase-local MDP, a specialized policy may approximate the local optimum πm⋆\pi_{m}^{\star} better than a finite shared policy trained across all phases, giving Gm>0G_{m}>0. This is a finite learning effect, not an expressivity advantage. Since, better phase-local policies need not achieve a better global return once handoffs are included, we isolate the settled comparison by evaluating both architectures on the same settled reference distribution μmref\mu_{m}^{\mathrm{ref}}.

Let J¯m⋆\bar{J}_{m}^{\star} and Πm⋆\Pi_{m}^{\star} denote the optimal quasi-stationary return in phase mm and its set of optimal policies. We measure the heterogeneity of phase mm by the loss incurred when policies optimized for other phases are transferred to it:

so HmH_{m} is large when behaviour optimal elsewhere performs poorly in phase mm; the supremum avoids dependence on an arbitrary choice of policy when a phase has several optima. For the shared and specialized architectures, define the phase-local learning gaps

εm,sh​(B,Hm)=J¯m⋆−𝔼⁡[J¯mqs​(π^sh,B,μmref)],εm,sp​(Bm)=J¯m⋆−𝔼⁡[J¯mqs​(π^m,sp,Bm,μmref)].\displaystyle\varepsilon_{m,\mathrm{sh}}(B;H_{m})=\bar{J}_{m}^{\star}-\mathbb{E}\!\left[\bar{J}_{m}^{\mathrm{qs}}(\widehat{\pi}_{\mathrm{sh},B};\mu_{m}^{\mathrm{ref}})\right],\quad\varepsilon_{m,\mathrm{sp}}(B_{m})=\bar{J}_{m}^{\star}-\mathbb{E}\!\left[\bar{J}_{m}^{\mathrm{qs}}(\widehat{\pi}_{m,\mathrm{sp},B_{m}};\mu_{m}^{\mathrm{ref}})\right].

which absorb finite capacity, data, exploration, optimization, and architectural bias. In particular, the shared εm,sp\varepsilon_{m,\mathrm{sp}} accounts for joint optimization challenges such as multi-task gradient dilution (App. A.1.5), whereas independent specialists avoid cross-phase gradient interference entirely. Writing HmH_{m} as an argument of εm,sh\varepsilon_{m,\mathrm{sh}} emphasizes that the shared learner must fit phase-mm behaviour jointly with other phases, without assuming any particular functional dependence. The expected settled specialization gain is then exactly

Gm,refqs=εm,sh​(B,Hm)−εm,sp​(Bm).G_{m,\mathrm{ref}}^{\mathrm{qs}}=\varepsilon_{m,\mathrm{sh}}(B;H_{m})-\varepsilon_{m,\mathrm{sp}}(B_{m}). (7)

Heterogeneity HmH_{m} widens εm,sh\varepsilon_{m,\mathrm{sh}}, while data pooling transferable representations across phases narrows it. Specialization eliminates this joint capacity bottleneck, but each specialist receives only a fraction ζm∈(0,1)\zeta_{m}\in(0,1) of the total sample budget BB, i.e., Bm=ζm​BB_{m}=\zeta_{m}B, or B/MB/M under uniform allocation ζm=1/M\zeta_{m}=1/M. A specialist ensemble therefore achieves Gm,refqs>0G_{m,\mathrm{ref}}^{\mathrm{qs}}>0 only when the local sample allocation Bm=ζm​BB_{m}=\zeta_{m}B avoids data starvation by exceeding the phase-local sample threshold B0,m​(δ)B_{0,m}(\delta) required for a target suboptimality tolerance δ>0\delta>0 (App. A.1.4, Prop. 4).

4.3 From Regime Quantities to Architecture Choice

The advantage presented in (4) becomes predictive when the regime quantities are bounded, either by environment analysis or by short pilot runs. Substituting bounds G¯m≤Gm≤G¯m\underline{G}_{m}\leq G_{m}\leq\overline{G}_{m} and K¯m≤Km≤K¯m\underline{K}_{m}\leq K_{m}\leq\overline{K}_{m}, yields certified bounds on relative performance:

R¯:=∑mωm​[(1−λm)​G¯m−λm​K¯m]≤Δ​J¯≤∑mωm​[(1−λm)​G¯m−λm​K¯m]=:R¯.\underline{R}:=\sum_{m}\omega_{m}\left[(1-\lambda_{m})\underline{G}_{m}-\lambda_{m}\overline{K}_{m}\right]\leq\Delta\bar{J}\leq\sum_{m}\omega_{m}\left[(1-\lambda_{m})\overline{G}_{m}-\lambda_{m}\underline{K}_{m}\right]=:\overline{R}. (8)

Hence R¯>0\underline{R}>0 certifies specialization, i.e., J¯​(π^sp)>J¯​(π^sh)\bar{J}(\widehat{\pi}^{\rm sp})>\bar{J}(\widehat{\pi}^{\rm sh}), and R¯<0\overline{R}<0 certifies sharing. An interval containing zero leaves the choice unresolved and favours an intermediate architecture (i.e., a multihead network, although (8) compares only the shared and specialized endpoints and does not certify that option. For a specific phase mm with G¯m>0\underline{G}_{m}>0 and K¯m≥0\overline{K}_{m}\geq 0, specialization yields a positive local lower bound whenever the transient fraction satisfies:

λm<G¯mG¯m+K¯m.\lambda_{m}<\frac{\underline{G}_{m}}{\underline{G}_{m}+\overline{K}_{m}}. (9)

so the settled gain must persist long enough to amortize the transient handoff cost. Table 2 summarizes the resulting regimes. The specialized bound dominates when the settled gain outweighs the handoff and budget penalties, and the shared bound when transfer, scarce phase-local data, or boundary sensitivity is decisive; multihead suits the unresolved region because it preserves shared features while allowing phase-specific action mappings.

5 Experiments and Results

To test the regime model of Sec. 4, we evaluate PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) on three phase-structured environments: high-altitude platform systems (HAPS) coverage optimization Loussouarn et al. (2026), PhasePendulum, and PhaseGridWorld, all described in detail in App. A.3.2, App. A.3.3, and App. A.3.4, respectively. In the HAPS network, the idea is to find the optimal position of the HAPS given that the user density and traffic vary over time but in a periodic manner. In particular, different phases inside a period are differentiated by different user densities and traffic loads. The entire service region of the HAPS network is divided into multiple cells; only a few selected cells act as hotspots where the user density and traffic are higher than the rest of the cells. PhasePendulum environment consists of the standard torque-controlled pendulum dynamics while changing the target angle gmg_{m} between phases. PhaseGridWorld environment is a 9×99\times 9 grid with four deterministic actions: up, down, left, and right. Each phase has its own goal and obstacle map. All environments are periodic, with the number of phases and cycles varying by experiment. We compare three architectures: a single policy with the phase and clock augmentation, a multipolicy of MM specialists, and a multihead policy with a shared trunk and MM heads. All methods use the same PPO hyperparameters unless stated otherwise, and we report raw reward per environment step throughout. We organize the results around four hypotheses (H1 to H4) obtained from Sec. 4 and presented in Table 2.

Our three main methods span different degrees of parameter sharing. Single+clock is a single actor–critic taking physical state, phase index, and within-phase clock as inputs. Multihead receives the physical state and phase index and combines a shared actor body and a shared critic with MM phase-specific linear action heads; at each step the head indexed by the active phase emits the action, so the shared body is updated from every transition while each head is updated only from transitions of its own phase. The phase code is also supplied to the body, allowing it to form phase-conditioned features rather than only phase-agnostic ones. Multipolicy uses MM independent actor–critics, the active phase selecting which one acts and is updated; its input is the physical state, whereas the clock-aware variant is denoted multipolicy+clock. The phase code is not supplied here, since selecting the network already identifies the phase. More details on the methods can be found in App. A.3.1

5.1 H1: Longer Phases Favour Specialization with multi-policy

In the HAPS environment, the transient regime is governed by platform relocation and by user persistence across phase boundaries. A direct transit takes at most 100100 steps when both spatial coordinates of the HAPS change maximally, and mean user lifetimes of 55 to 2525 steps are much shorter, so we take Lm≈100L_{m}\approx 100. Reward differences arise mainly when one or two platforms fail to reach a high-density zone, so any difference between two policies should be in the same order. Following this observation, Gm≈KmG_{m}\approx K_{m} reduces (9) to λm<1/2\lambda_{m}<1/2, and with γ≈1\gamma\approx 1 and λm≈Lm/Tm\lambda_{m}\approx L_{m}/T_{m} this predicts a crossover at T≈2​Lm=200T\approx 2L_{m}=200. We treat 200200 as a diagnostic horizon rather than a strict value of TmT_{m}, since arrivals are stochastic and learned trajectories need not be straight. The prediction is that shared policies win below this dwell time, where the transient dominates, and specialized policies above it, where the quasi-stationary regime does. Fig. 2 (left), at M=20M=20, shows exactly this: multipolicy reward increases with TT, Single+Clock decreases, the two curves cross near T=200T=200, and multihead is largely insensitive to TT, confirming its position as an in-between solution. PhasePendulum reproduces this pattern (Table 11). For both M=5M=5 and M=10M=10, the single policy leads at T∈{100,200}T\in\{100,200\} while multi-policy attains the best mean at T=500T=500; multi-head performs very close to multi-policy and even surpasses in some cases. Longer dwell times therefore favour specialization wherever a quasi-stationary regime is physically reachable.

5.2 H2: Behavioural Diversity Increases the Burden on Single Shared Policy

Heterogeneity can be increased by adding distinct phases, which leaves each specialist’s problem unchanged while requiring the shared policy to represent more behaviours. Fig. 2(right) reports the performance of the HAPS for different phase counts at T=500T=500: Single+Clock degrades as MM grows while multi-policy is flat, so the effect is a degradation of complete sharing rather than a benefit of more phases. The snapshots in Fig. 8 in the appendix show the mechanism, with the shared policy failing to reach the hotspots of some phases. Widening the shared network or using four, six or eight layers does not close the gap, and a network with eight layers performs worse than one with six layers (Table 6). The shared policy therefore does not fail for lack of parameters: adding them does not help and can hurt. Its limitation lies in training rather than in representational capacity, as Prop. 2 implies, so the remaining gap is an architectural advantage for multipolicy. PhasePendulum varies behavioral diversity more directly, setting target angles to gm​(h)=h​gmmaxg_{m}(h)=h\,g_{m}^{\max} (App. A.3.3). Table 10 reports hh from 00 to 11. The single policy is best at h=0h=0, where all phases are identical, and at h=0.25h=0.25; from h=0.5h=0.5 the ordering reverses, with multihead first and multipolicy second. Heterogeneity therefore widens the shared learner’s gap as in (7), far enough to reverse the advantage of sharing. In PhaseGridWorld (Fig. 13), where handoff costs are negligible, shared and specialized architectures perform comparably when adjacent phases share an optimal policy, while multipolicy clearly outperforms the shared baseline when they require distinct ones. Heterogeneity alone therefore suffices to separate the architectures.

We test whether the single-policy degradation observed above is caused by destructive shared updates in Table 9 and Fig. 9. The orthogonal-null alignment statistic AgA_{g} presented (App. A.1.5) remains close to one for any MM. Thus the main reason behind learning degradation is not the destructive interference. It explains why gradient surgery solutions such as PCGrad/CAGrad did not close the gap with multipolicy in our environments, as gradient destruction is not the biggest burden (Table 5). The cosine similarity falls from 0.6750.675 to 0.1950.195 for complete sharing as MM grows from 22 to 2020 (Table 9), close to the 1/M1/\sqrt{M} orthogonal benchmark derived in App. A.1.5.

With more distinct phases in the shared policy, the cosine similarity is going to decrease for larger MM. We call this effect gradient dilution. Together with the capacity controls, it shifts the explanation toward finite approximation and shared optimization burden.

5.3 H3: Specialization Requires Sufficient Phase-Local Data

Under a fixed total interaction budget BB, a balanced multipolicy allocates only Bm≃B/MB_{m}\simeq B/M samples to specialist mm. Shared PPO instead updates one model from all BB interactions. We call failure to reach a high-return local solution within BmB_{m} the learning starvation; this concerns finite-budget performance, not optimizer convergence.PhasePendulum at h=0h=0 isolates this effect because all ten phases are identical and any performance gap must reflect optimization and sample efficiency rather than representation capacity. With a total budget of B=5​MB=5\text{M} timesteps, each redundant specialist receives a partitioned allocation of only Bm≈500​kB_{m}\approx 500\text{k} interactions. As shown in Fig. 11, Single+clock strongly outperforms Multipolicy because local specialists suffer from severe sample starvation (Bm<B0,mB_{m}<B_{0,m} App. A.1.4), failing to reach local convergence. Fig. 10 confirms this threshold behavior: Multipolicy requires a total budget scaling to B≥10​MB\geq 10\text{M} for each local allocation to cross B0,mB_{0,m} and approach the asymptotic performance level of Single+clock. A single-phase GridWorld calibration provides consistent evidence (Tab. 12): the clock-aware shared model reaches the target learning threshold within 500​k500\text{k} interactions across all three seeds, whereas the multipolicy model requires a total 750​k750\text{k} steps to reliably match it. It is important to note the intrinsic advantage of adding clock information to any solution (Sec. A.4.3). Also, Tab. 15 illustrates that increasing the global budget can invert the performance ranking between single and multipolicy models.

5.4 H4: Handoff Dependence Can Reverse the Ranking

Studying handoff dependence is challenging in general because transient regimes are rarely cleanly delimited in complex tasks. We address this by using controlled GridWorld environments where the underlying causality is fully understood. Because independent specialists optimize phase-local objectives from local resets, they lack awareness of downstream continuation values, incurring a boundary coordination loss. Full-trajectory shared policies can instead sacrifice immediate phase return to ensure the overall highest return (Prop. 3).

Fig. 7 formalizes this trade-off in a two-phase GridWorld. Selecting an immediate goal (g00g_{00}, reward 1.01.0) leaves the agent trapped behind an impassable wall in Phase 1, whereas selecting a safe goal (g01g_{01}, reward ρ<1.0\rho<1.0) preserves Phase 1 reachability. As shown in Fig. 12 (ρ→0.9\rho\to 0.9), Single+clock and Multihead adapt to choose g01g_{01} in almost all episodes. In contrast, independent specialists (Multipolicy) remain myopic, selecting g00g_{00} in 90%90\% of episodes and failing Phase 1 entirely. Here, the transient regime length equals the full phase duration (Lm=TmL_{m}=T_{m}), completely annihilating specialization gains due to uncoordinated local policies.

A second GridWorld experiment (App. A.3.4) evaluates the transient regime across two dimensions: (1) varying phase goals and wall layouts to adjust phase heterogeneity and coordination demands, and (2) comparing physical state carryover against resampling from reachable entry states (Fig. 6). As shown in Fig. 13, physical carryover severely penalizes Multipolicy in the irrecoverable Closed Trap (Lm=TmL_{m}=T_{m}). Resetting phase entry to a common reachable state eliminates boundary costs (Km≈0K_{m}\approx 0), reversing to a positive gap for Multipolicy. Conversely, in the recoverable Bottleneck (Lm<TmL_{m}<T_{m}), Multipolicy dominates under both physical carryover and reachable resets.

6 Conclusion

We have investigated when phase-structured reinforcement learning should employ a single shared policy versus phase-specific multiple-policies. Given sufficient scheduler information, single and multiple policies have the same representational capability, so any difference in performance must come from the environment and the learning dynamics rather than from representation. The proposed regime decomposition of the phases helps to understand the difference between single and multiple policies under constraints such as limited samples, phase-heterogeneity, and the mutual coupling between phases. We observe that sharing is favoured when phases exhibit behavioral overlap, learning budgets are constrained, or boundary-state coordination consumes a large fraction of the phase duration. Specialization is favored when phases are heterogeneous, per-specialist data volume is sufficient, and the quasi-stationary gain exceeds the handoff cost. Partially shared designs, e.g., multihead networks offer a intermediate solution between these two extremes.

Future work should look beyond the binary choice between single shared and specialized multi policy models. The key challenge lies in designing adaptive architectures that share transferable features, specialize where local optimization is hard. and propagate continuation values across phase boundaries. Extending this framework to unknown phase structures and develop a coordinated multiple policies provide a promising foundation for a new class of phase-structured RL algorithms.

Appendix A Appendix

The appendix is organized in four parts. Sec. A.1 defines the optimization, heterogeneity, capacity, budget, and handoff quantities used by the regime framework, and then assembles the predictive certificate. Sec. A.2 groups the complete derivations by their role in the argument. Sec. A.3 specifies the environments, training protocols, and reporting conventions. Sec. A.4 contains additional quantitative results and qualitative diagnostics.

A.1 Supporting Mechanisms and Bounds

This section provides the definitions and results used by the different sections of this work.

A.1.1 Schedule Sufficiency and Markovian Augmentation

To model phase transitions formally within the MDP framework, the physical state st∈𝒮s_{t}\in\mathcal{S} must be augmented with scheduler information zt∈𝒵z_{t}\in\mathcal{Z}. Formal Markovian Sufficiency Condition.

We define the scheduler state ztz_{t} as sufficient if the joint transition dynamics satisfy:

Pr(st+1∈A,zt+1∈B∣s0:t,a0:t,z0:t)=Pσ⁡(t)(A∣st,at)q(B∣zt),\Pr(s_{t+1}\in A,z_{t+1}\in B\mid s_{0:t},a_{0:t},z_{0:t})=P_{\sigma(t)}(A\mid s_{t},a_{t})\,q(B\mid z_{t}), (10)

for all measurable sets A⊆𝒮A\subseteq\mathcal{S} and B⊆𝒵B\subseteq\mathcal{Z}, where Pm(⋅∣s,a)P_{m}(\cdot\mid s,a) is the transition kernel of phase mm, and q(⋅∣zt)q(\cdot\mid z_{t}) is the exogenous schedule update kernel. When Equation (10) holds, the augmented state s~t=(st,zt)\tilde{s}_{t}=(s_{t},z_{t}) forms a time-homogeneous Markov Decision Process ℳ~=(𝒮×𝒵,𝒜,P~,r~,γ)\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}=(\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{Z},\mathcal{A},\widetilde{P},\widetilde{r},\gamma). A.1.2 A Transient–Quasi-Stationary View

We now split each phase into an early transient period and a later settled quasi-stationary period. Let pmπ​(t)p_{m}^{\pi}(t) be the state-transition probabilities induced by policy π\pi at time step tt. Let W1W_{1} be the Wasserstein-1 distance that is used to measure how far the current distribution is from the settled one in units of distance on the state space.
